title: Thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy and DIC
definition: Thrombocytopenia is found in almost every dog with babesiosis and rarely causes bleeding. A smaller group, mostly with complicated B. rossi disease, has a consumptive coagulopathy: low clotting factor and inhibitor activities, longer PT and aPTT and higher D-dimer, with fibrin microthrombi in organs at necropsy, read by the authors as DIC [R1][R2][R3].
definition_note: Changed. The working definition treated thrombocytopenia and DIC as one bleeding spectrum. The literature separates them: thrombocytopenia is the rule and seldom bleeds, while consumptive coagulopathy is a marker of severe, often fatal disease whose main lesion is microthrombosis rather than haemorrhage. No babesiosis study used a validated canine DIC score; DIC was inferred from marker panels [R1][R2][R4][R5].
key_points: Expect a low platelet count: it is present in nearly all dogs, often below 40 x10^9/L, and on its own seldom causes bleeding [R6][R7][R3].

With antibabesial treatment the count returns to normal within about a week in uncomplicated B. rossi and by the second imidocarb dose, about 17 days later, in B. canis; it needs no specific treatment unless the dog bleeds [R8][R9][R10].
In B. rossi, the platelet count does not separate survivors from non-survivors; longer PT, low antithrombin and low factor VII and X activities do [R11][R1][R2].
B. rossi dogs keep near-normal clot strength on thromboelastography because fibrinogen is high; the danger is microthrombosis and organ failure, not haemorrhage [R12][R1].

Bleeding with prolonged clotting times is treated with plasma; bleeding with normal clotting times and a very low count may be secondary immune thrombocytopenia, for which a short prednisone course is suggested by expert review [R10][R13].
No anticoagulant, antiplatelet or antifibrinolytic drug has been tested for survival in dogs with babesiosis.

description.heading: What it is
description.text: Three overlapping states occur. Isolated thrombocytopenia, usually without bleeding signs, is the commonest [R3][R11]. An activated, procoagulant state with raised thrombin-antithrombin complexes and low antithrombin occurs even in uncomplicated B. canis disease [R4][R14]. A consumptive coagulopathy with factor loss, inhibitor consumption, reduced fibrinolysis and organ microthrombi is found mainly in dogs that die [R1][R2].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: Thrombocytopenia was found in 99.5% of 248 dogs with large Babesia in Poland, in all 49 B. canis dogs in Germany, and in all 86 B. rossi dogs in a Pretoria study [R6][R7][R8]. Suspected DIC was recorded in 12 of 46 German B. canis dogs [R7]. In an Indian series selected for bleeding signs, 23.8% of B. gibsoni dogs were grouped as pancytopenia with DIC, with criteria not stated in the abstract [R15].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: Changes are present at admission, before treatment [R1]. In B. rossi the platelet count rose within 24 to 48 hours of treatment in survivors and the median count was normal by day 6 in the 46 uncomplicated dogs still sampled [R11][R8]. In B. canis the count was normal in 21 of 23 dogs at the second imidocarb injection, about 17 days after the first [R9]. B. rossi non-survivors died at a median of 24 hours [R1].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: Severe inflammation activates coagulation: thrombin is generated, antithrombin and protein C are consumed, and fibrinolysis is suppressed [R1][R14]. High fibrinogen and large, activated platelets keep clot strength near normal despite few platelets [R12][R3]. Platelet loss is thought to be partly immune-mediated: counts recover quickly, and platelet-bound antibodies were found in 11 of 33 tested B. canis dogs [R8][R7]. These mechanisms are proposed, not proven.

species_notes.note: Most data come from one Onderstepoort group. Uncomplicated dogs are normocoagulable on TEG; non-survivors show factor consumption, low antithrombin and microthrombi [R3][R1][R2].
Procoagulant markers in uncomplicated dogs; aPTT prolonged in 34 of 39 tested dogs in Germany; a low platelet count was linked to death in one small study [R14][R7][R16].
aPTT prolonged in 10 of 17 tested dogs with normal PT; immune thrombocytopenia and bleeding are described in case reports [R17][R18].
One programme reports low fibrinogen and raised fibrin monomer and degradation products, unlike the high fibrinogen of B. rossi; species were not typed [R5][R19].

criteria.note: Lower limit of the Onderstepoort reference interval used in B. rossi studies; reference intervals differ between laboratories.
Cut-off used in 49 German B. canis dogs; 39 dogs were below it and 2 of them bled.

criteria.threshold: longer PT and aPTT, lower factor and protein C activities, higher D-dimer than survivors
criteria.note: Comparisons of medians at admission; no single cut-off was published. In one cohort non-survivors had median PT 7.6 s, antithrombin 62%, factor VII 49% and factor X 42%.

criteria.criterion: DIC as diagnosed in babesiosis studies
criteria.threshold: raised thrombin-antithrombin with low antithrombin; or raised fibrin monomer, fibrin degradation products and D-dimer with low fibrinogen
criteria.note: Marker panels interpreted by the authors; no formal score was applied in any babesiosis study found.

criteria.threshold: model based on aPTT, PT, D-dimer and fibrinogen
criteria.note: Sensitivity 91% and specificity 90% in development, 83% and 77% in validation, in dogs in intensive care. Not tested in babesiosis; coefficients are in the paywalled paper.

clinical_signs.note: The usual picture: none of 19 uncomplicated B. rossi dogs with a median count of 20 x10^9/L bled.

clinical_signs.sign: Petechiae and ecchymoses on skin and mucous membranes
clinical_signs.note: 7 of 50 dogs (14%) in a Ukrainian series of untyped Babesia.
Epistaxis in 3 of 15 B. canis dogs in Switzerland; single dogs in other series and case reports.

clinical_signs.sign: Signs of organ thrombosis or infarction
clinical_signs.note: Found at necropsy: microthrombi in 8 of 12 B. rossi non-survivors (heart, lung, spleen, liver, kidney, brain).

tests.test: Platelet count with blood smear review
tests.finding: Low count; check the smear for clumps and confirm a very low count manually.
tests.note: Studies excluded samples with platelet aggregation and confirmed low automated counts by hand.
Did not differ between survivors and non-survivors in B. rossi.

tests.finding: aPTT often mildly prolonged; PT longer in B. rossi non-survivors.
tests.note: Interpret against the laboratory's own interval. aPTT was shortened in one B. canis study on days 2 and 3.

tests.finding: High fibrinogen and mildly raised D-dimer in B. rossi; antithrombin low, lowest in non-survivors.
tests.note: Laboratory tests; low fibrinogen was reported only from untyped dogs in Ukraine.

tests.finding: Near-normal clot strength with slow initiation and reduced lysis in B. rossi.
Positive in 11 of 33 tested B. canis dogs.
tests.note: Specialist laboratory test; supports a secondary immune mechanism.

differentials.distinguish: PCR or serology. In the Eastern Cape co-infection was found in 3 of 149 B. rossi dogs, and thrombocytopenia did not predict it.

differentials.condition: Evans syndrome or secondary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia (SY02)
differentials.distinguish: Agglutination, spherocytes, Coombs test with thrombocytopenia.
Low leucocyte and red cell counts with low platelets; 19 of 46 B. canis dogs were pancytopenic.

differentials.condition: Other causes of prolonged clotting times (for example anticoagulant rodenticide)
differentials.distinguish: History; a hypocoagulable TEG with very long clotting times.

grading.criteria: Platelets below 30 x10^9/L (B. gibsoni, Hong Kong laboratory). A German B. canis study used below 40 x10^9/L.

approach.action: Count platelets and look for bleeding
approach.detail: Confirm a very low count on a smear. Examine skin, gums, sclera, nose, urine and faeces for bleeding. Most dogs will not bleed [R3][R7].

Start antibabesial treatment (TX00). Expert review advises against immunosuppression based on the count alone; base it on clinical signs [R10]. In treated survivors the count rose within 24 to 48 hours [R11][R8].

approach.action: Test clotting in sick or bleeding dogs
approach.detail: In complicated disease or with bleeding, measure PT and aPTT, and fibrinogen, D-dimer and antithrombin where available. Prolonged PT with consumption points to a worse prognosis in B. rossi [R2][R1].

approach.action: Bleeding with prolonged clotting times: give plasma
approach.detail: Fresh frozen plasma was used for bleeding dogs with prolonged clotting times in case reports and series; refer for repeated plasma, platelet products or TEG [R10][R7][R13].

approach.action: Bleeding with normal clotting times and a very low count
approach.detail: Consider secondary immune thrombocytopenia. Expert review suggests a short prednisone course if bleeding continues despite antibabesial treatment [R10].

approach.action: Count still low after one to two weeks
approach.detail: This is outside the course seen in treated B. rossi and B. canis. Recheck for persistent infection and test for Ehrlichia co-infection, although it was uncommon in the Eastern Cape [R8][R9][R21].

treatments.name: Fresh frozen plasma
treatments.aim: Replace consumed clotting factors and inhibitors in a bleeding dog with prolonged clotting times.
treatments.evidence_summary: Expert review states that dogs with DIC or coagulation disorders may need plasma [R10]. Four of 49 German B. canis dogs with prolonged clotting times received one plasma transfusion each; outcome was not reported by treatment [R7]. A B. gibsoni dog with DIC was stabilised with blood and plasma [R13]. No babesiosis source gives a dose; the dose below is from dogs with other hypocoagulable disorders [R23].

doses.frequency: once in 2 dogs; in 1 dog continued to a total of 15 mL/kg after a repeat TEG
doses.context: 3 dogs given plasma (rodenticide, angiostrongylosis, DIC after systemic inflammation) in a case series of 4 (not babesiosis)
doses.note: Volume chosen by TEG after in vitro plasma addition. The fourth dog, with immune thrombocytopenia, gained nothing from plasma on TEG and got whole blood.

treatments.cautions: One dog had a mild reaction (muzzle and eyelid oedema) after a total of 15 mL/kg, which responded to an antihistamine [R23]. Not indicated for a low platelet count without bleeding [R10].
treatments.monitoring: Bleeding, PT and aPTT, and TEG where available, after each unit [R23].

treatments.name: Fresh whole blood or platelet products
treatments.aim: Supply platelets and factors, with red cells, to a dog that is bleeding and anaemic.
treatments.evidence_summary: One German B. canis dog with severe thrombocytopenia and prolonged clotting times received platelet-rich plasma; no outcome was reported for it [R7]. No study measured whether whole blood or platelet products change outcome in babesiosis. Red cell transfusion is covered in SY01. The dose below comes from a non-babesiosis series of thrombocytopenic dogs [R24].

doses.frequency: per transfusion; median 2.5 transfusions (range 1 to 13) per dog
doses.context: Thrombocytopenic dogs with haematocrit below 0.20 L/L (20%), given before romiplostim, retrospective series of 42 dogs (not babesiosis)
doses.note: Given for anaemia caused by bleeding; the same series gave 10 mL/kg packed red cells as the alternative. Effect on platelet count not reported.

treatments.cautions: No babesiosis data on adverse effects or on platelet increments after transfusion [R7].
treatments.monitoring: The source series monitored haematocrit and platelet count; no schedule for babesiosis is published [R24].

treatments.name: Glucocorticoids (prednisone or prednisolone) for secondary immune thrombocytopenia
treatments.aim: Reduce immune platelet destruction in a dog that bleeds despite antibabesial treatment.
treatments.evidence_summary: In a small randomised trial in 18 B. gibsoni dogs with immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia, mean platelet count rose to normal by day 21 in the arm without prednisolone as well as in the arms with it; groups were not compared statistically [R22]. Expert review suggests prednisone only for bleeding or high risk with platelets of 20 to 40 x10^9/L despite antibabesial treatment, for ten days or less [R10]. Case reports combine it with other drugs [R18].

doses.context: Expert recommendation, European review of canine babesiosis
doses.note: Only for moderate to severe signs despite antibabesial treatment, such as collapse or spontaneous bleeding; dose reduction may be faster than in primary disease.

doses.context: B. gibsoni with immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia, 6 dogs in this arm, randomised trial
doses.note: Given with doxycycline, metronidazole and clindamycin. The source PDF text is split; the dose follows the prednisolone-only arm in text order.

treatments.cautions: Expert review notes that immunosuppression is controversial because the cause is infectious, and that dogs on long-term immunosuppressants respond less well [R10].
treatments.monitoring: Platelet count and bleeding; the sources give no schedule [R10][R22].

treatments.name: Dextran with dipyridamole infusion
treatments.aim: Reduce platelet and red cell aggregation and restore circulating volume in shock with DIC.
treatments.evidence_summary: One Ukrainian programme in untyped large Babesia compared a plasma substitute alone (10 dogs) with the same solution plus dipyridamole (10 dogs) and reported better laboratory aggregation and haemodynamic values over 72 hours with the mixture [R25]. A second report from the same programme (100 dogs) used a dextran with dipyridamole mixture [R19]. Allocation was not described, outcomes were laboratory values only, and survival was not reported.

doses.drug: Reosorbilact plasma substitute 100 mL mixed with dipyridamole 0.5% 4 mL
doses.context: Untyped large Babesia, 10 dogs, non-randomised controlled trial
doses.note: Ukrainian products. Group allocation not described; laboratory outcomes only.

doses.dose: 5 mL/kg of the mixture (45 mg dextran and 2.5 mg dipyridamole per kg)
doses.context: Untyped Babesia, 100 dogs in the study, number treated not stated (abstract)
doses.note: Composition as stated in the abstract.

treatments.cautions: Colloid and antiplatelet effects in a thrombocytopenic dog were not assessed for bleeding in these reports.
treatments.monitoring: Platelet count, blood pressure and haematocrit, as in the source studies.

treatments.name: Romiplostim
treatments.aim: Stimulate platelet production in severe immune thrombocytopenia.
treatments.evidence_summary: A B. gibsoni dog with urogenital bleeding and immune thrombocytopenia recovered with romiplostim, prednisolone and antibabesial drugs [R18]. In a retrospective series of 42 thrombocytopenic dogs, the one babesiosis dog improved, but the authors credit antimicrobial treatment as a possible cause; 2 of 6 dogs with DIC improved, which the authors attribute more to DIC management than to romiplostim [R24].

doses.frequency: single dose in most dogs; up to 4 doses
doses.context: Thrombocytopenia of various causes, 42 dogs, retrospective series (one with babesiosis)
doses.note: One dog received 3 µg/kg. In the 27 dogs that improved, median time to platelets above 50 x10^9/L was 4 days.

treatments.cautions: Few data in dogs; the series reported it as well tolerated [R24].
treatments.monitoring: Platelet count until recovery, as in the source series (median 4 days to above 50 x10^9/L in responders) [R24].

treatments.name: Vincristine
treatments.aim: Speed platelet recovery in severe immune thrombocytopenia.
treatments.evidence_summary: No use in babesiosis was found. In 24 bleeding dogs with severe primary immune thrombocytopenia, one dose with prednisone raised the count to 40 x10^9/L or more faster than prednisone alone (mean 4.9 versus 6.8 days) and shortened hospital stay [R26].

doses.context: Severe primary immune thrombocytopenia, 12 dogs in this arm, prospective controlled study, not randomised (not babesiosis)
doses.note: Given with prednisone 1.5 to 2 mg/kg PO every 12 h. Prednisone-only dogs that did not respond got vincristine on day 7.

treatments.cautions: No adverse effects were attributed to vincristine in the trial [R26]. Its relevance to infection-associated thrombocytopenia is unknown.
treatments.monitoring: Platelet count, transfusion need and outcome, as in the trial [R26].

treatments.name: Heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight)
treatments.aim: Limit microthrombosis and consumption of clotting factors.
treatments.evidence_summary: Not tested in dogs with babesiosis. Reviews mention heparin for DIC and as thromboprophylaxis in secondary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia [R10]. The B. rossi authors propose treatments that target thromboinflammation as future research [R1]. In an experimental B. canis infection, heparin injections were followed by a transient rise in parasitaemia, read as release of sequestered parasites [R27]. Canine dosing protocols are in a consensus guideline that was not available in full text [R28].
treatments.cautions: Antithrombin activity is low in B. rossi, lowest in non-survivors [R1]. The bleeding risk of heparin in dogs with severe thrombocytopenia from babesiosis has not been studied.
treatments.monitoring: The consensus guideline recommends therapeutic monitoring when unfractionated heparin is used [R28].

prognosis.text: Thrombocytopenia alone has a good outlook once the parasite is treated [R8][R9]. In B. rossi, 12% to 18% of dogs in coagulation cohorts died; non-survivors had consumptive coagulopathy and lower haematocrit, not lower platelet counts. Deaths include euthanasia for poor prognosis [R1][R2]. In general canine DIC, hypocoagulable dogs died more often than hypercoagulable dogs (64% versus 32%) [R29].

indicators.meaning: No prognostic value: median 34 x10^9/L in survivors and 32 in non-survivors; platelet indices also did not differ.
Associated with death in 15 dogs (sensitivity and specificity 83%); lactate and leucocyte count were better markers.

indicators.finding: Longer PT, low antithrombin, low factor VII and X (B. rossi)
Low factor and protein C activities and high D-dimer (B. rossi)

indicators.meaning: Higher case fatality than hypercoagulable TEG; not studied in babesiosis.

related.why: The drugs against the parasite; treating the infection is what restores the platelet count.
Red cell transfusion and severe anaemia.
Evans syndrome and secondary immune-mediated haemolytic anaemia.
Complicated disease, triage and the order of care.

evidence_gaps: No babesiosis study applied a validated canine DIC score, so the frequency of overt DIC is unknown.
No trial in dogs with babesiosis tested plasma, platelet products, heparin, antiplatelet drugs or glucocorticoids against survival.
No source on tranexamic acid, aspirin or clopidogrel in canine babesiosis was found; B. rossi dogs already show reduced fibrinolysis.
Whether the low counts are immune-mediated, consumptive or due to sequestration has not been settled.
The coagulation profile of B. vogeli and of PCR-typed B. canis in South Africa is not described.
What a platelet count that stays low after treatment means, and how often it reflects co-infection, was not studied.
The dextran with dipyridamole reports come from one programme with untyped parasites and laboratory outcomes only.

search.note: Local review notes and full texts, then PubMed searches on babesiosis with DIC, plasma, heparin and thrombocytopenia treatment, and on canine immune thrombocytopenia, DIC scoring, transfusion and tranexamic acid. The CURATIVE dosing paper and the canine DIC score paper were paywalled and read as abstracts. Platelet-index and endothelial-marker studies without clinical use were left out.
